analysis.one_liner: Opens more of the Gulf of Mexico to offshore oil and gas leasing and speeds up drilling permits.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: all five of its sponsors were Republicans, the Energy and Natural Resources Committee held one hearing in May 2015, and the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Interior Department to offer at least half of the most promising unleased federal acreage in the Gulf of Mexico for oil and gas drilling, and to hold three new lease sales in the eastern Gulf near Florida in 2018, 2019, and 2020. It would have shrunk a no-drilling buffer off Florida's coast from 125 miles to 50, shared up to roughly $1 billion a year of federal drilling revenue with Gulf states, and shortened or removed several steps that currently slow drilling permits, environmental reviews, and court challenges.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would gain mandated access to new Gulf acreage, faster permit deadlines, limits on environmental review, and a shorter, narrower path for opponents to sue. Gulf state governments would also gain, since the bill directs 50 percent of certain federal offshore revenues into a fund shared with the states, capped at $999 million per year from 2026 through 2055.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf oil companies and Gulf state governments

how_it_helps.text: Requires Interior to offer at least 50% of the most resource-rich unleased Gulf acreage for sale in each five-year leasing plan, and to include any Gulf planning area holding more than 2.5 billion barrels of oil or 7.5 trillion cubic feet of gas.

Mandates three new lease sales in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico in 2018, 2019, and 2020, and moves the no-drilling 'Military Mission Line' so the area off Florida closed to drilling shrinks from 125 miles to 50 miles from the coast.

Sends 50% of qualified federal offshore revenues from areas near Gulf producing states to the states, capped at $500 million in 2017, $699 million per year from 2018 to 2025, and $999 million per year from 2026 to 2055, with 25% of the shared share going to land and water conservation.

Imposes deadlines on the National Marine Fisheries Service for marine mammal 'incidental harassment' permit requests and treats unanswered requests as automatically approved, and extends the window for a company to keep a lease in continuous production from 180 to 270 days.

Narrows environmental review for the new lease sales — Interior would not have to analyze a no-leasing alternative — and channels all challenges to drilling decisions into a single court, with a 60-day deadline to sue and a 180-day deadline for the court to rule.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, coastal communities and fishing and tourism businesses near the newly opened eastern Gulf would have borne the risk of spills and drilling activity closer to shore. Federal taxpayers would have borne the cost of giving up a share of federal offshore revenue, up to roughly $1 billion a year, and the weakened environmental review and shortened court deadlines would have reduced the public's ability to scrutinize and challenge drilling decisions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities, fisheries, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill would have cut the no-drilling buffer off Florida's coast from 125 miles to 50 miles, putting drilling activity and spill risk much closer to beaches and fishing grounds that anchor Florida's coastal economy.

For the new lease sales, Interior would not have been required to identify nonleasing alternatives or analyze the environmental effects of alternatives under the National Environmental Policy Act — a major narrowing of the review the public normally gets before drilling is approved.

The bill would have given opponents of a drilling decision only 60 days to sue, limited them to a single court with a 180-day clock, and cut off all other courts from hearing the claims, making legal challenges to drilling much harder to bring and win.

Marine mammal protection would have been weakened: permit requests for activities that may harm marine mammals would have had to be decided on fixed deadlines, and a request the agency failed to answer in time would automatically be treated as approved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine benefits — drilling revenue for Gulf state budgets and more domestic energy production — came bundled with a heavy tilt toward industry: mandated lease sales written into statute, a shrunken Florida buffer, environmental review reduced to a single preferred alternative, and court challenges squeezed into a 60-day window in one court. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill traded public oversight and coastal risk protection for producer certainty and state revenue, and that the Gulf's own experience with the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill made the coastal risk case particularly pointed. Its failure means no one had to make that trade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2015 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held a hearing but never sent it to the full Senate, so it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on May 11, 2015, with four Republican cosponsors — Sens. Vitter, Wicker, Cornyn, and Cochran — and it was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on May 19, 2015 (S.Hrg. 114-118), but the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the Senate or the House.

The bill's lease-sale mandates and revenue-sharing provisions would have required amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006, which never happened during the 114th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the offshore oil industry did not gain the mandated Gulf lease sales or the shortened permitting and legal deadlines, and coastal and fishing interests near the eastern Gulf were spared drilling moving closer to shore. The other side of the coin: Gulf state governments never received the expanded revenue share the bill promised, and the nation did not get the additional production it would have mandated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities; the oil industry missed out

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Senate Republicans; because the bill never reached a floor vote, the record shows no roll-call and no recorded opposition from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated lease sales covering at least half the most promising unleased Gulf acreage, forced three sales in the eastern Gulf, shortened permit and marine mammal review deadlines, narrowed environmental review, and channeled court challenges into a single 60-day window — a package written around producer certainty. The public cost was spill risk near Florida's coast and reduced oversight.

industries.industry: Gulf state governments (LA, TX, MS, AL, and FL)
industries.note: The bill would have directed 50% of qualified federal offshore revenues into a fund shared with Gulf producing states, capped at $999 million per year from 2026 through 2055, with a quarter of the shared share going to land and water conservation. This revenue would have flowed to state budgets serving those states' residents.

industries.industry: Gulf coastal tourism, fishing, and seafood businesses
industries.note: Shrinking the eastern Gulf no-drilling buffer from 125 miles to 50 miles would have moved drilling near beaches, fishing grounds, and seafood waters, exposing those industries and their workers to spill and disruption risk. Their interest ran with the coastal residents who depend on an undeveloped shoreline.
